newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO says Bosnian Serb retaliation will fail.
newsitem.headline: NATO says Bosnian Serb retaliation will fail.

text.p: NATO commander Wesley Clark said on Wednesday that Bosnian Serb revenge attacks would not deter the alliance from enforcing the country's peace treaty.

The U.S. general made clear in a speech in Sarajevo that the NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) would adhere to a tougher policy towards indicted war criminals despite Serb retaliatory violence against international observers and peacekeeping soldiers.
"Let there be no misunderstanding. SFOR will fulfil its mandate in every respect. There is no turning back," said Clark, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander.
"We will not be deterred or intimidated. If threatened or blocked, we will take strong action."

Two U.S. soldiers and one Dutch trooper have been wounded in a wave of retaliatory bombings and other low-level violence this month since NATO pounced on two Serbs wanted by the United Nations war crimes tribunal.
Clark spoke at a military ceremony marking the arrival of the new SFOR commander, U.S. General Eric Shinseki, who echoed Clark's warnings.
Shinseki told reporters the violence was "not wise" and that his troops were ready to defend themselves if necessary.
"Our soldiers have a mandate for self-defence and it would be unfortunate for someone to miscalculate and end up being a serious casualty when our soldiers employ their weapons..." Shinseki said.
Shinseki, who was wounded in combat in the Vietnam war, formally assumed command of SFOR three weeks after the arrest operation broke new ground for the mission.

NATO had previously ruled out going after war crimes suspects unless peacekeeping troops encountered them during their regular duties. But Western countries decided to shift tactics to try to remove fugitives sabotaging the peace process.

The raid and the introduction of sealed, or secret, indictments has spread anxiety among nationalist Serb leaders and other warlords who fear losing their grip on power and lucrative smuggling rackets.
Retaliatory violence in Serb territory has tapered off over the past several days after NATO officers and Western diplomats delivered stern warnings to Serb hardliners.
NATO spokesmen said the alliance made no offer to call off further arrests of indicted war criminals, including the most prominent, former Bosnian Serb President Radovan Karadzic.
The wartime Serb leader charged with crimes against humanity continues to wield power behind the scenes in Serb territory from his headquarters in Pale, outside Sarajevo.
British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook delivered a tough message on the war crimes issue to Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of the collective presidency, in a visit to Bosnia on Tuesday.

Cook said that the West would not allow indicted war criminals to undermine the peace agreement but Krajisnik, a staunch Karadzic ally, told reporters that Serb authorities regarded the U.N. tribunal in The Hague as a political tool.

British soldiers seized and extradited one suspect in this month's raid and shot dead another who opened fire. The suspect who was arrested, Milan Kovacevic, pleaded not guilty on Wednesday in The Hague on charges of complicity in the commission of genocide against Moslems and Croats.
